lessons.title: Kaiser Wilhelm and the difficulties of ruling Germany

before.content_html:
In 1890 Germany was barely twenty years old as a unified country — and already the strain was showing. On the surface it looked like a modern industrial power with a written constitution and an elected parliament. Underneath, real power sat with one man: Kaiser Wilhelm II. Understanding how power was shared (or, more accurately, how it was not) is the foundation for everything that follows in this period.

The Empire Wilhelm Inherited

Germany only became a single country in 1871, when Otto von Bismarck stitched together twenty-five states under the leadership of Prussia. The constitution he wrote handed enormous power to the Kaiser. The Kaiser commanded the army, controlled foreign policy, appointed the Chancellor, and could dissolve the elected parliament whenever it became inconvenient. Bismarck had used this system skilfully for nineteen years, balancing the competing interests of socialists, Catholics, industrialists and aristocrats.

In 1890, the new Kaiser dismissed Bismarck. Wilhelm II was twenty-nine, ambitious and determined to be his own Chancellor. The men who replaced Bismarck — Caprivi, Hohenlohe, then Bernhard von Bülow from 1900 — were weaker, more pliable figures. Power drifted upwards to the throne, and important decisions were increasingly taken by the Kaiser and a small circle of advisers rather than negotiated through parliament.

Key Fact

Under the 1871 constitution the Kaiser commanded the army, controlled foreign policy, appointed the Chancellor and could dissolve the Reichstag. The Reichstag was elected but could only debate budgets and laws — it could not appoint or sack the government.

The Reichstag, the Bundesrat and the Limits of Democracy

Germany did have an elected lower house, the Reichstag, chosen by all men over 25. By European standards in 1890 this was a wide franchise. The catch was that the Reichstag had no power over the executive. It could approve or refuse the budget and pass laws, but it could not choose the Chancellor or remove him. That decision belonged to the Kaiser alone.

Above the Reichstag sat the Bundesrat, an upper house made up of representatives sent by the twenty-five states. Prussia, the largest state by population and territory, held seventeen of its fifty-eight seats — enough to veto any change to the constitution. In effect, Germany was a federation in which Prussia could always say no.

A bill needed approval from both the Reichstag and the Bundesrat, then assent from the Kaiser. If the Reichstag voted down a budget the Chancellor often simply ruled by emergency decree. If the Reichstag became too troublesome the Kaiser could dissolve it and call a fresh election. Real influence did not run upwards from voters — it ran downwards from the throne, through the Chancellor, to the parties.

Prussian Dominance and the Junkers

Prussia was not just the largest state — it was the most conservative. Its parliament was elected by a three-class voting system that gave the wealthiest men votes worth seventeen times those of the poorest. This kept Prussian politics dominated by the Junkers, the aristocratic landowners east of the river Elbe. The Junkers ran the army, the senior civil service and most of the diplomatic corps. The Kaiser himself was the King of Prussia. So when southern, more liberal states such as Bavaria or Baden tried to push reform, Prussian votes in the Bundesrat usually blocked them.

Wilhelm II spoke openly of his belief in the divine right of kings. He wore military uniform almost every day and surrounded himself with generals. This atmosphere of Prussian militarism set the tone of the whole government. To advance in the imperial civil service or court life, an officer's commission was almost essential.

An Industrial Giant Outgrowing Its Politics

While the political structure stayed locked in 1871, the economy was transforming. By 1900 Germany produced more steel than Britain. Coal output doubled between 1890 and 1914. Cities such as Berlin, Hamburg and Essen grew rapidly as peasants moved off the land into factories. The population rose from 49 million in 1890 to 68 million by 1914.

Industrial growth produced two new political forces the old constitution struggled to absorb. First, the urban working class, which voted in huge numbers for the Social Democratic Party (SPD). Second, a confident middle class of engineers, lawyers and businessmen who wanted a real say in government. By 1912 the SPD was the largest single party in the Reichstag — yet not one of its members ever sat in Wilhelm II's cabinet.

Bismarck had managed the contradictions through twenty years of practice. Wilhelm II had no such patience. He chopped between policies, sacked ministers, gave inflammatory interviews to foreign newspapers, and lost the trust of even his own conservative allies after the 1908 Daily Telegraph affair. Chancellor Bülow resigned in 1909; his successor, Theobald von Bethmann-Hollweg, inherited a system where the Reichstag, the Junkers, the SPD and the Kaiser all wanted different things and none could outvote the others. By 1914 the political system was paralysed long before the war broke it.

Key Fact

By 1912 the SPD was the largest Reichstag party with over a third of the vote, yet no Social Democrat ever served as a minister under Wilhelm II. This gap between elected support and real government power is the central tension of pre-war German politics.

lessons.title: Impact of the First World War on Germany

before.content_html:
In August 1914 millions of Germans cheered the outbreak of war. By November 1918 sailors were mutinying, workers were striking and the Kaiser was on a train to Holland. Understanding how a confident empire collapsed in just over four years is essential because almost every problem of the Weimar Republic — reparations, the ‘stab in the back’ myth, hyperinflation — began here.

The Burgfrieden and the Mood of August 1914

When Wilhelm II declared war on Russia and France he announced that ‘I no longer recognise parties; I recognise only Germans’. The SPD agreed. On 4 August 1914 every party in the Reichstag, including the Social Democrats, voted for war credits. This political truce was called the Burgfrieden — literally ‘castle peace’ — meaning class and party conflict would be paused for the duration. Crowds in Berlin and Hamburg sang patriotic songs. For a few weeks Weltpolitik appeared to have done its job.

The unity rested on a short-war assumption. Generals expected Paris to fall in six weeks (the Schlieffen Plan). Workers expected a Christmas victory. When the war stalemated in muddy trenches that autumn, those expectations curdled. By 1916 fewer than half of military-age men remained outside uniform.

Key Fact

The Burgfrieden of August 1914 united the Reichstag — including the SPD — behind the war effort. It depended on the assumption of a short victory and broke down once stalemate, hunger and casualties exposed the gap between elite war aims and working-class suffering.

The Allied Blockade and the Turnip Winter

The Royal Navy began blockading German ports in August 1914. Germany imported about a third of its food before the war — fertiliser from Chile, grain from Russia, dairy from Denmark. The blockade cut all of that. Inside Germany, the army requisitioned horses, men and machinery away from farms. By 1916 food rations had been cut to roughly 1,000 calories a day for civilians, well below subsistence.

In the autumn of 1916 the potato crop failed. Civilians fell back on the only thing left: turnips, normally fed to livestock. The winter of 1916–17 became known as the turnip winter. Around 750,000 German civilians died of hunger or disease linked to malnutrition over the course of the war. Birth rates collapsed. Mothers queued for hours for bread.

The blockade was not just a foreign-policy tool. By starving urban Germany it broke the Burgfrieden from below. Workers struck for food in Berlin in April 1917 and again in January 1918, when over a million workers downed tools across major cities. The same workers had cheered for war in 1914. Their anger by 1917 was at the regime that had failed to feed them, not just at Britain or France.

War Weariness and Political Splits

By 1917 the SPD itself split. A breakaway party, the Independent SPD (USPD), refused further war credits. From the USPD's far-left fringe came the Spartacus League, led by Karl Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg, calling for revolution. Strikes spread. Soldiers home on leave reported that civilians on trains and in queues now openly criticised the war. Inflation made things worse: by 1918 the mark had lost half its 1914 value.

From 1916 the army effectively ran the country. Field Marshal Paul von Hindenburg was Chief of the General Staff with Erich Ludendorff as his deputy. They imposed a ‘silent dictatorship’, directing factories, food rationing and even Reichstag debates by sheer force of military prestige. Civilian Chancellors became figureheads.

The Spring 1918 Offensive and Defeat

Russia's collapse in 1917 freed German divisions for one final gamble. In March 1918 Ludendorff launched a massive offensive on the Western Front. It made the largest gains of the war — but stalled forty miles from Paris when American troops arrived in numbers. From August 1918 the Allies counter-attacked. By late September the German army was in retreat. Ludendorff lost his nerve and told the Kaiser the war was lost.

Crucially, this conversation happened privately. The German army was still on French and Belgian soil. To civilians, defeat seemed sudden and unexplained. This gap — between an army that had not been beaten in battle on home ground and a government suddenly suing for peace — would later be exploited by the right-wing ‘stab in the back’ myth.

Ludendorff insisted that civilian politicians, not generals, sign the armistice. He wanted the army's reputation untouched and the blame placed elsewhere. In late October a new civilian government under Prince Max of Baden took office, and on 9 November the SPD's Philipp Scheidemann proclaimed a republic from a Reichstag balcony. The same day the Kaiser fled across the border into the neutral Netherlands. Within forty-eight hours the SPD's Friedrich Ebert had signed the armistice on 11 November 1918.

Kiel, Revolution and the Republic

The trigger was the navy. In late October 1918 admirals at Kiel ordered the High Seas Fleet to sea for one last battle. Sailors refused. The mutiny spread along the coast. Workers’ and soldiers’ councils, modelled on Russia's soviets, sprang up in Hamburg, Munich and Berlin. The empire collapsed in less than a week. Wilhelm II, abandoned by his army, abdicated on 9 November after his generals told him the troops would no longer fight for him.

In four years Germany had gone from cheering crowds to revolutionary councils, from confident empire to mutinous republic. Every problem the new democracy would face — food shortages, returning soldiers, the ‘stab in the back’ lie — had its roots in this collapse.

Key Fact

When the armistice was signed on 11 November 1918 the German army was still on French and Belgian soil — retreating, but not crushed. The hidden truth that Ludendorff had told the Kaiser the war was lost in late September made the right-wing ‘stab in the back’ myth possible, blaming civilian politicians for a military collapse the generals had concealed.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1919 right-wing pamphlet arguing the German army was undefeated and was ‘stabbed in the back’ by socialist politicians) and Interpretation B (a modern textbook arguing Germany was militarily exhausted and starving by November 1918) on why Germany lost the First World War. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A claims military defeat was caused by political betrayal — civilian leaders signed an armistice while the army was still on French soil.
• Interpretation B claims defeat was caused by exhaustion — the spring 1918 offensive failed, troops were retreating, and the home front had collapsed under blockade and food shortages.
• Main difference: A blames civilians and revolutionaries; B blames structural collapse on both fronts.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): difference identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one side only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1919 right-wing pamphlet promoting the ‘stab in the back’ theory) and Interpretation B (a modern textbook on the home-front collapse) give different views about Germany's defeat in 1918.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different purposes — the 1919 pamphlet aimed to discredit the new Weimar government; the modern textbook aims for balanced explanation.
• They use different evidence — the pamphlet relies on the fact that German troops were still in France; the textbook uses casualty figures, food statistics and the Kiel mutiny.
• They were produced at different times — the 1919 pamphlet had political motives in the immediate post-war crisis; the textbook has access to archives, including private generals' memoirs.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: 'Germany's defeat in 1918 was decided not at the front but in the queues for bread, the soup kitchens and the strike halls of the home front.' How convincing is Interpretation A about the reasons for Germany's defeat in the First World War?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because the Allied blockade triggered the 1916–17 turnip winter and roughly 750,000 civilian deaths from hunger-linked illness, breaking civilian morale.
• Convincing because the January 1918 strikes, with over a million workers, foreshadowed the Kiel mutiny that ultimately ended the monarchy.
• Less convincing because the spring 1918 Ludendorff offensive failed for military reasons — American troop arrivals, supply shortages and Allied counter-attacks — not just home-front pressure.
• Less convincing because Ludendorff himself accepted defeat in late September 1918 because of military collapse, not bread queues; the home front then collapsed afterwards.
• Overall judgement: home front and front-line collapse were tightly linked — the interpretation is partly convincing but underplays the army's exhaustion.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Allied blockade on Germany between 1914 and 1918.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Cut imports of food and fertiliser, reducing rations to roughly 1,000 calories a day for civilians by 1916 and contributing to the turnip winter of 1916–17 in which the potato crop failed.
• Caused approximately 750,000 civilian deaths from hunger-linked disease and a sharp fall in birth rates, especially in working-class urban districts.
• Drove industrial unrest — the April 1917 Berlin strike and the January 1918 strike of over a million workers across major cities directly cited food and peace as demands.
• Helped break the Burgfrieden by exposing the gap between the elite (still well-fed) and the working class, paving the way for the SPD split and the rise of the USPD.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific figures and dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of how the First World War destroyed the German monarchy by November 1918.
You may consider:
• the impact of military defeat in 1918
• the impact of the home-front collapse and the Kiel mutiny.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Military exhaustion: the spring 1918 Ludendorff offensive failed and Allied counter-attacks from August 1918 forced the German army back; Ludendorff told the Kaiser the war was lost.
• Civilian leadership replaced military leadership: a new government under Prince Max of Baden took office in October 1918 to negotiate peace.
• Home-front collapse: the blockade, turnip winter, 750,000 civilian deaths and January 1918 strikes destroyed loyalty to the regime.
• Kiel mutiny (late October 1918): sailors refused a final death-or-glory mission; revolt spread to Hamburg, Munich and Berlin within days; workers' and soldiers' councils replaced state authority.
• Abdication: with the army no longer reliable and the SPD demanding a republic, Hindenburg told the Kaiser the troops would not fight for him; Wilhelm fled to Holland on 9 November 1918.
• Conclusion: military defeat made peace inevitable, but it was the home-front collapse and Kiel mutiny that turned defeat into republican revolution — the two reinforced each other.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and a substantiated judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail; judgement may be limited. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1925 SPD memoir crediting the November 1918 revolution to the working class and the Kiel mutineers) and Interpretation B (a 1923 conservative writer arguing the abdication was forced on the Kaiser by his own generals) on the cause of Wilhelm II's abdication. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A locates the cause in popular revolution from below — sailors refused to fight, councils sprang up, workers' strikes finished the regime.
• Interpretation B locates the cause at the top — Hindenburg and the army told the Kaiser the troops would not stay loyal, removing his last protection.
• Main difference: A emphasises bottom-up popular agency; B emphasises top-down elite calculation.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

lessons.title: Post-war problems and the Treaty of Versailles

before.content_html:
The young Weimar Republic faced three connected post-war crises that almost destroyed it before it had finished writing its constitution. Reparations made Germany a debtor nation overnight. The 1923 Ruhr occupation stripped its industrial heartland. Hyperinflation in the same year wiped out savings and pensions. By the autumn of 1923 a loaf of bread cost 200 billion marks. Understanding why these crises happened — and who they hurt — is essential because right-wing parties, including the Nazis, would feed off this trauma for the next decade.

The Treaty of Versailles, June 1919

Germany was not invited to negotiate. Allied delegates handed German representatives a 440-article treaty in May 1919 with no real opportunity to bargain. To Germans this made it a diktat, a dictated peace. The terms were severe: Germany lost Alsace-Lorraine to France, the Saar coalfield to Allied control, parts of Posen to Poland, and all of its overseas colonies. The army was capped at 100,000 men, conscription was banned, the Rhineland was demilitarised, and tanks, submarines and an air force were forbidden.

The two clauses Germans hated most were Article 231, the ‘war guilt clause’ making Germany accept responsibility for starting the war, and the open-ended commitment to reparations. The exact figure was set by an Allied commission in 1921: 132 billion gold marks, payable over 42 years.

Key Fact

The Treaty of Versailles imposed territorial losses (Alsace-Lorraine, the Polish Corridor, all colonies), military restrictions (army capped at 100,000; no air force; demilitarised Rhineland), financial costs (132 billion gold marks reparations from 1921), and moral burden (Article 231 war guilt). Together these gave the political right a permanent grievance against Weimar democracy.

The Stab in the Back Myth and the November Criminals

The new Republic had to sign Versailles or face renewed Allied invasion. Foreign Minister Hermann Müller signed the treaty on 28 June 1919. Right-wing parties immediately branded the SPD-led government the ‘November Criminals’ for accepting the armistice and Versailles. The Dolchstosslegende — the legend that the army had been ‘stabbed in the back’ by socialists, Jews and democrats — spread quickly. It mattered because it transferred the blame for losing the war from the generals (where it belonged) to the politicians who had to pick up the pieces.

In August 1921 right-wing assassins murdered Matthias Erzberger, the Centre Party politician who had signed the armistice. In June 1922 they killed Walter Rathenau, the Jewish Foreign Minister who had pursued reconciliation with the Allies. Political violence was running ahead of any agreed national strategy for paying reparations.

Economists then and now disagree. Germany was the largest economy in continental Europe in 1919 even after war losses. The bill of 132 billion gold marks was painful but not impossible — spread across forty-two years it was around 6–7% of national income, broadly comparable to French reparations after 1871. The deeper problem was political: paying meant accepting Versailles, raising taxes on the rich, and losing voters. So instead Weimar governments printed money to cover the gap.

The Ruhr Occupation, January 1923

Germany missed reparations payments in late 1922. France's Prime Minister Raymond Poincaré chose enforcement over renegotiation. On 11 January 1923 French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr valley — Germany's industrial heartland, producing 80% of its coal and steel. The plan was to seize coal, coke and timber by force.

Chancellor Wilhelm Cuno's government called for passive resistance. Workers went on strike. Trains stopped. Mines lay idle. Berlin paid the strikers from central government funds. There was sporadic sabotage; 132 Germans were killed in clashes with French troops. The occupation lasted until late 1923 and cost both sides far more than it produced — the French got little coal; the Germans lost industrial output and tax revenue.

Hyperinflation

To pay strikers without crushing the rest of the economy, the Reichsbank simply printed paper marks. Inflation already running since 1919 became a runaway collapse. Hyperinflation peaked in November 1923. A loaf of bread that cost 250 marks in January 1923 cost 200 billion marks by November. Workers were paid twice a day. Restaurants printed menus in pencil so prices could be updated. The dollar bought 4.2 trillion marks at the peak.

Hyperinflation did not hurt all Germans equally — this nuance is what examiners want to see. Losers: pensioners on fixed incomes saw savings vanish; war widows lost government allowances; small savers lost everything in the banks; landlords on long leases were ruined. The middle-class Mittelstand — clerks, civil servants, teachers — lost most because their identity rested on respectable savings. Winners: anyone with debts (mortgages, business loans) saw them effectively cancelled; large industrialists like Hugo Stinnes bought up smaller firms cheaply; farmers with land kept producing food and barter; manual workers in employment generally kept their jobs. The middle class lost both their savings and their faith in the Republic. Many would later vote Nazi.

The Crisis Ends

In August 1923 Gustav Stresemann became Chancellor. He called off passive resistance in late September, accepting that the Ruhr struggle could not be won. In November he introduced a temporary new currency, the Rentenmark, backed by a mortgage on land and industry. One Rentenmark equalled one trillion old paper marks. The currency stabilised because Germans, exhausted, agreed to trust it. Reparations were renegotiated through the 1924 Dawes Plan.

The political damage stayed. The middle class never forgot 1923. The far right had its grievance machine fully assembled. And Adolf Hitler — whose Munich Putsch attempt on 8–9 November 1923 almost coincided with the inflation peak — had received his first national publicity.

Key Fact

Hyperinflation was contained within a year by the Rentenmark, but the damage to middle-class trust in Weimar democracy lasted a decade. Voters who lost savings in 1923 carried that grievance into the Depression elections of 1930–33.
before.exam_tip_html: Examiners punish students who claim hyperinflation hurt all Germans equally — you must show who lost (savers, pensioners, the middle class) and who gained (debtors, industrialists, sometimes manual workers in jobs). For the 8-mark Evaluate an Interpretation question, watch for sources that simplify the Treaty of Versailles as either the cause of all later problems (Nazi argument) or a peace Germany could have absorbed (some modern historians) — you need to weigh both. Lock in two date pairs: 1919 (Treaty signed) / 1921 (132 billion gold marks fixed), and Jan 1923 (Ruhr occupied) / Nov 1923 (Rentenmark issued). Precision lifts answers from generic to substantiated.

before.content_html:
Between January 1919 and November 1923 the new Weimar Republic faced four serious attempts to overthrow it. Two came from the far left, two from the far right. None succeeded, but each exposed weaknesses in the new democracy and shaped the political mood that would later carry Hitler to power. Examiners regularly flag that students confuse these uprisings — particularly the Spartacist rising and the Kapp Putsch — so chronological precision matters here.

The Weimar Constitution and Its Hidden Faults

In August 1919 a new constitution was signed in the small town of Weimar (chosen because Berlin was still volatile). It was, on paper, one of the most democratic in Europe. All adults aged 20 or over could vote, including women. There was a Bill of Rights guaranteeing free speech, religion and assembly. The President was elected directly. The Chancellor and his cabinet were responsible to the Reichstag.

The constitution had two structural weaknesses that examiners want students to spot. First, proportional representation meant that even tiny parties won Reichstag seats. Coalition governments became fragile. Between 1919 and 1933 Germany had twenty-one different cabinets, averaging seven months each. Second, Article 48 let the President suspend civil rights and rule by emergency decree in a crisis. It was meant as a safety valve. By 1932 it would be used routinely to bypass parliament.

Key Fact

The Weimar Constitution gave universal suffrage at 20, a Bill of Rights and direct election of the President — one of the most democratic constitutions of its time. But proportional representation produced unstable coalitions, and Article 48 gave the President an emergency power that would later be abused to dismantle democracy.

The Spartacist Uprising, January 1919

The first attack came from the far left. The Spartacus League, led by Karl Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg, had broken away from the SPD during the war. Inspired by the Russian Revolution of 1917, they declared a German Communist Party (KPD) on 30 December 1918 and on 5 January 1919 launched an uprising in Berlin. Strikers occupied newspaper offices and railway stations and called for soviet-style government.

Friedrich Ebert, the SPD leader and acting head of state, was terrified that Bolshevism would seize Germany as it had Russia. He turned to the army's General Groener and to the Freikorps — right-wing paramilitary bands of demobilised soldiers. Within ten days the Freikorps had crushed the rising. On 15 January 1919 they captured Liebknecht and Luxemburg, beat them, shot them and dumped Luxemburg's body in a Berlin canal. Around 200 Spartacists were killed.

Ebert had saved the Republic from the left, but at a cost: he had put himself in the army's debt and let an unaccountable right-wing militia loose on Germany's streets.

The Spartacists never had majority support. The SPD itself, with millions of votes and trade-union backing, opposed them. Most workers wanted a parliamentary republic, not a Russian-style soviet. The Spartacists were also militarily out-organised — they were a few thousand against well-armed Freikorps. Liebknecht and Luxemburg's deaths left the new Communist Party leaderless and embittered. The SPD-KPD divide on the German left would never heal — a fault line that would help the Nazis rise unopposed in 1932–33.

The Kapp Putsch, March 1920

In March 1920 the right-wing Wolfgang Kapp, a journalist and nationalist politician, allied with army officer Walther von Lüttwitz to overthrow the Republic. Their immediate trigger was a government order disbanding the 5,000-strong Ehrhardt Brigade Freikorps. Instead of disbanding, the brigade marched on Berlin. The army refused to fire on them — General von Seeckt famously said ‘Reichswehr does not shoot at Reichswehr’. Ebert and his cabinet fled to Stuttgart.

Kapp declared himself Chancellor. The Republic survived because of the workers, not the army. The SPD called a general strike. Berlin shut down: no transport, no electricity, no water, no newspapers. Civil servants refused Kapp's orders. Within four days Kapp's regime collapsed. He fled to Sweden.

The aftermath was telling. Kapp himself died awaiting trial in 1922. Few of his fellow conspirators received serious sentences. Compare the leniency to the Spartacists: the same German judiciary that hanged left-wing rebels gave right-wing rebels suspended sentences. Political assassinations followed: Erzberger killed in 1921, Rathenau in 1922.

The Munich Putsch, November 1923

By autumn 1923 hyperinflation was at its peak and the Ruhr occupation was still grinding on. In Bavaria a small Munich-based party, the National Socialist German Workers’ Party (NSDAP), had grown to about 55,000 members. Its leader Adolf Hitler decided this was the moment to seize power. On the evening of 8 November 1923 he and General Erich Ludendorff burst into a beer hall where the Bavarian state commissioner Gustav von Kahr was speaking. Hitler fired a pistol into the ceiling and announced a national revolution.

It was a fiasco. Kahr promised support, then phoned the regular army the moment Hitler left the building. The next morning Hitler and Ludendorff led 2,000 Nazi supporters in a march on Munich's Feldherrnhalle. Bavarian state police opened fire. Sixteen Nazis and four police were killed. Hitler dislocated his shoulder fleeing and was arrested two days later.

The trial in February 1924 turned defeat into propaganda. The sympathetic Bavarian judge let Hitler give long speeches that were reported in newspapers across Germany. He was sentenced to five years in prison — the minimum — and served only nine months in a comfortable cell at Landsberg, where he dictated Mein Kampf. Ludendorff was acquitted entirely. The lessons Hitler took: do not try to seize power by force; build a mass party and win elections instead. The contrast with Spartacist sentences could not be sharper.

Key Fact

The Kapp Putsch failed because of a workers' general strike, not because the army or judiciary opposed it. The Munich Putsch failed because the Bavarian state turned on Hitler at the last moment — but his trial gave him a national platform he had previously lacked.

Memorise the two pairs: Spartacists / Liebknecht & Luxemburg / Freikorps crushed them, and Kapp / Lüttwitz / general strike defeated them. For the 8-mark Explain Effects question on Weimar's instability, link the leniency of right-wing courts to the rise of nationalist violence later. For 12-mark essays, weigh the structural weaknesses of the constitution against the political violence on the streets — both mattered, but for different reasons.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Weimar Constitution of August 1919 looked highly democratic but contained proportional representation and Article 48 — weaknesses that would later be exploited.
  • The Spartacist uprising (January 1919) was crushed by Freikorps with state backing; the Kapp Putsch (March 1920) was defeated by a workers’ general strike, not by the army.
  • The Munich Putsch (November 1923) was a fiasco that arrested Hitler within hours, but his five-month trial turned him from a regional agitator into a national figure.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1919 SPD government statement crediting the Freikorps with saving the Republic from Bolshevism) and Interpretation B (a modern textbook arguing Ebert's reliance on the Freikorps was a long-term mistake) on the use of the Freikorps in 1919. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the Freikorps as saviours — without them the Spartacist uprising would have brought soviet government and a second Russian Revolution.
• Interpretation B presents the Freikorps as a long-term threat — they were unaccountable right-wing militias whose later involvement in the Kapp Putsch and political assassinations damaged the Republic they had helped save.
• Main difference: A frames the Freikorps as an emergency necessity; B frames them as a strategic blunder.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1919 SPD government statement on the Freikorps) and Interpretation B (a modern textbook) give different views about the use of the Freikorps in early 1919.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different purposes — the 1919 SPD statement was justification at a moment of crisis when Bolshevism appeared to threaten Germany; the textbook offers reflective historical analysis.
• They use different evidence — the SPD statement focuses on the immediate Spartacist threat; the textbook integrates later events including Freikorps involvement in the Kapp Putsch and political murders.
• They were produced at different times — the 1919 source had no knowledge of what would follow; the modern source benefits from the full sweep of Weimar history.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the failed Kapp Putsch of March 1920 on Weimar Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Demonstrated army unreliability — General von Seeckt's refusal to fire on the rebels showed the Reichswehr could not be relied on to defend the Republic against the right.
• Showed the power of organised workers — the SPD-led general strike paralysed Berlin within days and forced Kapp to flee, proving working-class solidarity could save the Republic.
• Exposed judicial bias — few conspirators were properly punished; Kapp himself died awaiting trial; this leniency contrasted sharply with the rapid execution of Spartacist leaders the year before.
• Encouraged further right-wing violence — surviving Freikorps members carried out political assassinations of Erzberger (1921) and Rathenau (1922), normalising violence as a political tool.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific names and dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of the political unrest faced by the Weimar Republic between 1919 and 1923.
You may consider:
• threats from the far left and far right
• how the Republic survived these threats.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Far-left threat: Spartacist uprising in Berlin January 1919 — Liebknecht and Luxemburg called for soviet government and were crushed by Freikorps; communist short-lived republics in Bavaria followed.
• Far-right threat: Kapp Putsch March 1920 — Wolfgang Kapp and Lüttwitz used the Ehrhardt Brigade to seize Berlin; the army refused to defend the elected government.
• Munich Putsch November 1923 — Hitler and Ludendorff attempted to march on Munich; sixteen Nazis and four police were killed before the Bavarian state arrested Hitler.
• Survival mechanisms: Ebert allied with army and Freikorps in 1919; SPD called a general strike against Kapp in 1920; Bavarian state police defeated the Munich Putsch.
• Political assassinations: Erzberger 1921, Rathenau 1922 — persistent right-wing violence even between coups.
• Conclusion: the Republic survived each threat, but at the cost of compromises (using Freikorps, lenient courts) that weakened it for later crises — the threats reflected the constitutional and judicial weaknesses set up in 1919.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail; judgement may be limited. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1924 Bavarian newspaper editorial calling the Munich Putsch a near-miss that almost overthrew the Republic) and Interpretation B (a modern textbook describing the Munich Putsch as a fiasco that arrested Hitler within hours) on the seriousness of the November 1923 Munich Putsch. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the Putsch as a serious threat — 2,000 marchers, Ludendorff's prestige, and the chaos of hyperinflation made revolution genuinely possible.
• Interpretation B presents the Putsch as a failure — Bavarian police shot the marchers within minutes and Hitler was arrested two days later.
• Main difference: A emphasises the moment's potential; B emphasises the actual outcome.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Munich Putsch of November 1923 on the future of the Nazi Party.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: • Provided national publicity — the February 1924 trial was reported across Germany and let Hitler give long propaganda speeches in court that introduced him to a national audience. • Lenient sentencing rewarded extremism — Hitler was given the minimum five-year sentence and served only nine months at Landsberg; Ludendorff was acquitted entirely. • Allowed the writing of Mein Kampf — Hitler dictated his political programme during his comfortable Landsberg imprisonment, fixing Nazi ideology in print. • Forced strategic rethink — Hitler abandoned violent putsches in favour of building a mass electoral party, a strategy that would carry the Nazis to the Reichstag from 1928 onwards. [Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific names and dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. lessons.title: The Stresemann era — recovery and Weimar culture

before.content_html:
From the wreckage of November 1923 a different Germany emerged. By 1928 unemployment was below 1.4 million, foreign investment was flooding in, and Berlin was the cultural capital of Europe. Historians call the years 1924–1929 the ‘Golden Years’ or ‘Stresemann era’ after the Foreign Minister who steered the recovery. But how golden were they? The German historian Detlev Peukert argued Weimar was ‘dancing on a volcano’ — that the recovery was real but built on US loans that could be recalled at any moment. The 1929 Wall Street Crash would prove him right.

Stresemann: Pragmatist, Not Saviour

Gustav Stresemann became Chancellor in August 1923 at the height of hyperinflation. His chancellorship lasted only 100 days, but it was the most decisive 100 days in Weimar history. He called off passive resistance in the Ruhr in late September 1923, accepting that the strike could not be won. He then introduced the temporary new currency, the Rentenmark, in November 1923. One Rentenmark exchanged for one trillion old paper marks. The new currency was backed by a mortgage on land and industrial property, and Germans agreed to trust it.

In August 1924 the Rentenmark was replaced by the permanent Reichsmark, backed partly by gold reserves. Stresemann himself was pushed out as Chancellor in November 1923, but he then served as Foreign Minister in every government from 1923 until his death in 1929 — six years of continuity in a system famous for its instability.

Key Fact

The Rentenmark replaced the worthless paper mark in November 1923 (1 Rentenmark = 1 trillion old marks). It was itself replaced by the permanent Reichsmark in August 1924, ending hyperinflation. Stresemann then served as Foreign Minister from 1923 until his death in 1929.

The Dawes Plan, 1924

Reparations remained the political wound that would not close. Stresemann's strategy was to admit Germany could not refuse them but argue it could not pay them at the 1921 schedule. American banker Charles Dawes was invited to chair an international commission. The Dawes Plan of August 1924 set graduated payments — smaller in early years, rising as Germany recovered — and crucially provided 800 million gold marks in American loans to kick-start the economy.

Over the next five years roughly 25 billion marks of US capital flowed into Germany. Industry rebuilt. Berlin's U-Bahn extended. New housing replaced wartime slums. Industrial output passed 1913 levels by 1928. By 1928 Germany was paying reparations broadly out of US loans — a circular flow that worked only as long as American money kept arriving.

Locarno, the League and the Young Plan

Stresemann's foreign policy aim was to ease Germany back into the European system as a respected partner, not a defeated outcast. In October 1925 he signed the Locarno Treaties, in which Germany voluntarily accepted its western borders with France and Belgium. Crucially the treaties left the eastern borders — with Poland and Czechoslovakia — open to future revision. To Germans this hinted that Versailles could be peacefully chipped at.

In September 1926 Germany was admitted to the League of Nations as a permanent member of its Council, equal in rank with Britain, France, Italy and Japan. In 1928 Germany signed the Kellogg-Briand Pact renouncing war as an instrument of policy — alongside fifteen other major powers.

The Young Plan of 1929, named after another American banker (Owen Young), reduced reparations from 132 billion gold marks to 112 billion and stretched payments to 1988. The political right hated it because it accepted reparations existed at all; right-wing parties including the small Nazi Party joined a referendum campaign against the plan in 1929. Their campaign lost — but it gave Hitler national exposure and respectable allies for the first time.

Examiner reports flag this confusion every series. The Dawes Plan (1924) restructured payments and brought in US loans — it did not reduce the total bill. The Young Plan (1929) actually cut the bill (from 132 to 112 billion) and stretched it to 1988. Dawes 1924 = restructure. Young 1929 = reduce. Memorise the pair as Dawes Restructure, Young Reduce.

Weimar Culture: Bauhaus, Brecht and Berlin Cabaret

As Germany stabilised politically, an extraordinary cultural flowering followed. Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus design school in 1919 — its modernist buildings, furniture and graphic design defined the era. Bertolt Brecht's plays (The Threepenny Opera, 1928) reinvented theatre. Berlin's cabarets, immortalised by Christopher Isherwood and later by the musical Cabaret, blended jazz, satire and sexual freedom unprecedented in European cities. The German film industry rivalled Hollywood: Fritz Lang's Metropolis (1927) and the first synchronised-sound film The Blue Angel (1930) were international hits.

For modernists this was liberation. For conservatives, particularly in rural Germany and the Catholic south, it was a moral collapse — what the Nazis later called ‘cultural Bolshevism’. Even some Weimar supporters worried that Berlin's cabarets and the Bauhaus's flat-roofed houses had little in common with how most Germans actually lived.

Limits of the Recovery

For all the headlines, the ‘Golden Years’ were patchy. Unemployment never fell below 1.3 million. Agriculture was already in depression by 1927 as world grain prices collapsed; small farmers struggled with debts. The recovery depended on US loans that could be recalled at three months’ notice. Coalition governments remained short-lived: there were six Chancellors between 1923 and 1929. President Friedrich Ebert died in 1925 and was replaced by 78-year-old Field Marshal Paul von Hindenburg — a war hero of the right who privately disliked the Republic he was now meant to defend.

Optimists like the historian Eberhard Kolb point to genuine industrial recovery, peace with neighbours, and democratic stability. Pessimists like Detlev Peukert argue the recovery was hollow — rural depression, dependence on US loans, an ageing right-wing President. The truth is mixed: Weimar genuinely recovered, but its recovery sat on foundations only as solid as the New York stock market. When Stresemann died on 3 October 1929, weeks before the Wall Street Crash, even contemporaries felt his death marked the end of the era. The streets of Berlin filled with mourners. Within five months of Wall Street's collapse, German unemployment doubled.

Key Fact

Stresemann's recovery rested on three pillars: a stable currency, US loans through the Dawes Plan, and diplomatic reintegration through Locarno and the League. All three were genuine achievements — but the second was beyond German control, which is why the 1929 Wall Street Crash hit Germany harder than any other major economy.
