lessons.title: The Depression and the rise of the Nazis, 1928-1932

before.content_html:
In May 1928, three months before the Wall Street Crash, the Nazi Party polled 2.6% in the Reichstag election. By July 1932 it polled 37.4% and was the largest party in Germany. Nothing about the Nazi programme had changed in those four years — what changed was the world economy. The Great Depression handed Hitler the votes that the Munich Putsch had failed to seize by force. Examiner reports flag this every series: it was the Depression that caused Hitler's rise, not the other way around. Direction of causation matters.

The Wall Street Crash, October 1929

On 24 October 1929 (‘Black Thursday’) the New York Stock Exchange collapsed. By the following Tuesday share prices had lost a quarter of their value. American banks called in their international loans — including those that had funded German industry under the Dawes Plan. Germany had borrowed roughly 25 billion marks of US capital between 1924 and 1929. Almost overnight that flow reversed.

The result was the deepest economic collapse Germany had ever experienced. Industrial production fell by 40% between 1929 and 1932. Banks failed. By 1932 over six million Germans were unemployed — about a third of the workforce. Many more were on short-time work. Soup queues stretched through major cities. Young men in particular saw no prospect of work; many drifted into Communist or Nazi paramilitary units which offered uniforms, food and a sense of purpose.

Key Fact

The Nazi Party rose from 12 Reichstag seats in 1928 to 230 seats in July 1932 — a thirteenfold rise in four years. The cause was the Depression, not Nazi policy: the party's programme had not changed. Nazi support actually fell to 196 seats in November 1932, showing the surge was unstable.

Bruning and the Politics of Austerity

In March 1930 the SPD-led grand coalition collapsed over how to fund unemployment insurance. President Hindenburg appointed the Centre Party's Heinrich Bruning. Bruning had no Reichstag majority. Instead Hindenburg used Article 48 of the constitution to let him rule by emergency decree. Five separate emergency decrees passed in 1931 alone. Bruning's policy was deflation: cut wages, cut benefits, cut government spending. He believed this would force prices down, restore competitiveness and let Germany trade its way out.

It made the Depression worse. Cutting benefits when six million were unemployed simply meant more starvation and more political extremism. Bruning was nicknamed the ‘Hunger Chancellor’. By 1932 the use of Article 48 had become routine: Hindenburg passed 66 emergency decrees compared to only five Reichstag laws. Weimar parliamentary democracy was effectively dead before Hitler ever became Chancellor.

Hindenburg was 84 by 1932 and surrounded by a small camarilla of right-wing advisers including his son Oskar and General Kurt von Schleicher. They saw the Depression as an opportunity to build an authoritarian government that bypassed the SPD altogether. Article 48 had been designed as an emergency safety valve in 1919; under Hindenburg it became a routine governing tool. This was the political space the Nazis would exploit: a President willing to govern without parliament, a Chancellor pursuing austerity that immiserated millions, and a Reichstag that no longer functioned.

The Nazi Surge, 1930–1932

In the September 1930 Reichstag election the Nazi vote leapt from 2.6% to 18.3%. The party won 107 seats, becoming the second-largest party. The Communists (KPD) also doubled their vote, reaching 13.1%. Together the two extreme parties controlled almost a third of the Reichstag. The political centre — SPD, Centre, liberals — was being squeezed from both sides.

In April 1932 Hitler stood for President against Hindenburg. He lost, but won 36% of the vote in the second round — not bad for a man who had only become a German citizen in February 1932. In July 1932 Reichstag elections he polled 37.4% and won 230 seats, becoming the largest single party. By this point the Nazi vote had grown thirteenfold in four years. But it had not grown enough: the Nazis still needed coalition partners or a presidential appointment to take power.

The Role of the SA

The Nazi vote was secured on the streets as well as at the ballot box. The SA (Sturmabteilung), led by Ernst Röhm after his return from Bolivia in 1930, grew from around 100,000 in 1930 to roughly 400,000 by July 1932 — larger than the Reichswehr army. SA ‘brownshirts’ broke up Communist and SPD meetings, marched in uniformed columns through working-class districts, and provided street muscle at every Nazi rally.

Crucially, the SA also offered welfare the state had stopped providing. Soup kitchens, dormitories, free uniforms and a sense of belonging drew unemployed young men in. By 1932 over half the SA was unemployed. Street violence escalated: in the summer of 1932 alone around 100 people were killed in Nazi–Communist clashes. To frightened middle-class voters this looked like civil war — and the Nazis successfully painted themselves as the only force capable of restoring order.

Hitler offered different things to different audiences, held together by Joseph Goebbels's modern propaganda machine. To the unemployed: jobs, food, dignity, work creation. To the middle class: protection from Communism, restoration of order, recovery of lost savings. To farmers: subsidies and protectionism against cheap imports. To industrialists: an end to trade-union militancy and a commitment to rearmament. To nationalists: revision of Versailles. To everyone: Volksgemeinschaft, a unified national community transcending class. Goebbels's posters, films and modern aircraft tours (Hitler flew to twenty cities in five days during the 1932 campaign) reached audiences other parties could not.

November 1932: The Vote Falls

In November 1932 fresh elections were called. The Nazi vote fell from 37.4% to 33.1% — from 230 seats to 196. Party finances were desperate. Goebbels's diary recorded morale collapsing. The KPD vote rose by another two percentage points. If parliamentary politics had simply continued, the Nazi surge might have run out of steam. But by November 1932 parliamentary politics had ceased to function. Hindenburg's small circle of advisers were already negotiating a way to bring Hitler into a controlled cabinet. The Depression had not fixed itself; it had broken the political system in which moderates might have survived.

Key Fact

The Communist KPD also grew rapidly during the Depression — from 10.6% in 1928 to 16.9% in November 1932. Many middle-class Germans voted Nazi not from love of Hitler but from fear of a Bolshevik revolution. Bruning's austerity, the SA's street violence and the KPD's rise together convinced enough voters that only an authoritarian regime could restore order.
before.exam_tip_html: Two examiner trip-wires for this lesson. First, do not write that Hitler caused the Depression — the Depression caused Hitler's rise. Direction of causation matters and gets flagged every series. Second, do not assume the Nazis were always popular. They polled only 2.6% in 1928 and their vote actually fell from 37% to 33% between July and November 1932. For the 8-mark Evaluate an Interpretation question, watch for sources that overstate Hitler's appeal as the cause of his rise, when fear of Communism, Bruning's austerity and the SA's street violence all mattered too. Lock in the seat totals: 12 (1928), 107 (1930), 230 (July 1932), 196 (Nov 1932).

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1932 Nazi Party leaflet claiming Hitler offered the only solution to mass unemployment) and Interpretation B (a 1932 SPD newspaper editorial blaming Bruning's austerity for the depth of the Depression) on the cause of the political crisis of 1930–32. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the crisis as solvable only by Hitler — mass unemployment, dependency on US loans and political stalemate required a strong leader.
• Interpretation B presents the crisis as worsened by Bruning's deflationary policies — cuts to wages and benefits when six million were unemployed deepened the slump.
• Main difference: A frames the crisis as a leadership vacuum requiring Hitler; B frames it as policy failure that created political space for extremism.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1932 Nazi leaflet) and Interpretation B (a 1932 SPD newspaper editorial) give different views about the cause of the 1930–32 political crisis.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different audiences and purposes — the Nazi leaflet aimed to recruit voters frightened by unemployment; the SPD editorial aimed to defend the elected government against authoritarianism.
• They use different evidence — the leaflet cites unemployment figures and Hitler's leadership claims; the editorial cites Bruning's emergency decrees and Article 48 abuse.
• They were produced from different political positions — both written in 1932 but with opposing interests in how the crisis was interpreted.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: 'The 1929 Wall Street Crash and the Depression that followed were the single most important cause of Hitler's rise to power.' How convincing is Interpretation A about the rise of the Nazi Party between 1928 and 1932?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because the Nazi vote rose from 2.6% (12 seats) in 1928 to 37.4% (230 seats) in July 1932 — a thirteenfold rise that exactly tracked unemployment reaching six million.
• Convincing because Nazi policy did not change in this period — the surge was driven by external economic catastrophe, not by ideological conversion.
• Less convincing because Bruning's austerity worsened the Depression and made the political system uniquely vulnerable — a different Chancellor might have contained the Nazi rise.
• Less convincing because Nazi propaganda, SA street violence and fear of Communism all contributed; the Depression was the trigger but not the only cause.
• Less convincing because Nazi support actually fell from 37% to 33% by November 1932, suggesting the Depression alone was not driving an unstoppable rise.
• Overall judgement: substantially convincing as the trigger but understates the role of Bruning, propaganda and political miscalculation by Hindenburg's circle.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Wall Street Crash of October 1929 on Germany.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Triggered withdrawal of US loans — the 25 billion marks of capital that had funded German industry under the Dawes Plan was recalled, causing factories and banks to fail.
• Caused mass unemployment — industrial output fell by 40% between 1929 and 1932; six million Germans were jobless by 1932, about a third of the workforce.
• Destroyed political stability — the SPD-led grand coalition collapsed in March 1930 and Hindenburg appointed Bruning, who governed by Article 48 emergency decree.
• Drove voters to extremes — the Nazi vote rose from 2.6% in 1928 to 37.4% in July 1932; the Communist KPD also doubled, squeezing the political centre.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific figures and dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of why the Nazi Party grew rapidly in support between 1928 and 1932.
You may consider:
• the impact of the Depression and unemployment
• the role of Nazi propaganda, the SA and Hitler's appeal.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Depression as trigger: industrial output fell 40% (1929–32); six million unemployed by 1932; banks failed; soup queues stretched through major cities.
• Bruning's austerity worsened conditions: wage and benefit cuts deepened the slump; government by Article 48 alienated Reichstag voters; he was nicknamed the ‘Hunger Chancellor’.
• Nazi vote surge: 12 seats (1928) to 107 (1930) to 230 (July 1932) — biggest party in Reichstag.
• SA growth: from 100,000 in 1930 to 400,000 by July 1932; offered welfare and uniforms to unemployed young men; provided street muscle and the appearance of order.
• Propaganda and Hitler's appeal: Goebbels's modern campaigns; Hitler's aircraft tour of twenty cities; targeted messages to unemployed (jobs), middle class (anti-Communism), farmers (subsidies), industrialists (rearmament), nationalists (Versailles revision); unifying concept of Volksgemeinschaft.
• Limits: November 1932 vote fell to 196 seats; party finances collapsing.
• Conclusion: the Depression and Bruning's response provided the opportunity; Nazi propaganda, SA muscle and Hitler's targeted appeal converted that opportunity into votes — but the surge had peaked by November 1932 and only Hindenburg's appointment of Hitler in January 1933 prevented its decline.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail; judgement may be limited. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1933 conservative writer arguing middle-class fear of Communism drove voters to Hitler) and Interpretation B (a modern academic study arguing Goebbels's propaganda and Hitler's personal appeal were decisive) on why ordinary Germans voted Nazi between 1930 and 1932. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A emphasises negative motivation — voters were repelled by KPD growth and the threat of Bolshevik revolution.
• Interpretation B emphasises positive attraction — Goebbels's modern propaganda machine, Hitler's aircraft tours and his oratory created loyalty.
• Main difference: A frames Nazi voters as reluctant defenders against Communism; B frames them as actively persuaded by Nazi messaging.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

lessons.title: The failure of Weimar democracy and Hitler's appointment

before.content_html:
By the end of 1932 the Nazi vote was falling and the party was almost bankrupt. Yet on 30 January 1933 Adolf Hitler walked into the Reich Chancellery as the new Chancellor of Germany. The puzzle of this lesson is how a party that had just lost 34 Reichstag seats in November came to power eight weeks later. The answer is not that Hitler was ‘voted in’ — the Nazis never won an outright majority in a free election. He was appointed by an 85-year-old President after a sequence of backstairs deals between elite conservatives who believed they could control him.

The April 1932 Presidential Election

The crisis of 1932 began with the presidential election. Paul von Hindenburg, then 84, stood for re-election against Hitler. Hindenburg won the second round in April 1932 with 53% to Hitler's 36%, but the result shook the conservative establishment. Hitler had won 13 million votes and proved that the Nazi movement was a permanent feature of German politics.

Hindenburg disliked Hitler personally — he called him ‘the Bohemian corporal’ — but the President was now surrounded by a small group of right-wing advisers including his son Oskar and General Kurt von Schleicher. They concluded that the only way to govern without the SPD was to harness the Nazi vote inside a controlled cabinet.

Key Fact

Germany had four chancellors in twelve months: Bruning (until May 1932), Papen (June 1932), Schleicher (December 1932), Hitler (January 1933). Each was appointed by Hindenburg using Article 48; none commanded a Reichstag majority. By January 1933 parliamentary government had effectively ceased to function.

Papen's Cabinet of Barons, June 1932

In May 1932 Schleicher persuaded Hindenburg to dismiss Bruning and appoint Franz von Papen, an obscure Centre Party aristocrat with no Reichstag seat. Papen's cabinet was nicknamed the ‘Cabinet of Barons’ because nine of its eleven members were aristocrats. It had almost no support in the Reichstag — in a vote of confidence in September 1932, Papen lost 512 to 42.

Papen's most aggressive move was the ‘Preussenschlag’ of 20 July 1932 — he used Article 48 to dismiss the elected SPD-led Prussian state government and install himself as Reich Commissioner. This destroyed the largest democratic stronghold in Germany and removed an SPD-controlled police force that had been resisting Nazi street violence. Many historians see this as the decisive moment when Weimar democracy stopped defending itself.

In the July 1932 election the Nazis polled 37.4% and won 230 Reichstag seats — their high water mark. Hitler demanded the chancellorship. Hindenburg refused, telling Hitler to his face on 13 August 1932 that he would not appoint him to a presidential cabinet. Papen called fresh elections for November. The Nazi vote fell to 33.1% and 196 seats — a loss of 34 deputies and around two million votes. Communist support rose. Goebbels's diary recorded that party morale was collapsing and finances were near bankruptcy. If parliamentary politics had simply continued, the Nazi tide might have ebbed. It did not get the chance.

Schleicher's Failed Chancellorship, December 1932

In December 1932 Schleicher persuaded Hindenburg that he, rather than Papen, should now be Chancellor. Schleicher tried to build a ‘cross-front’ coalition by splitting Gregor Strasser's left wing of the Nazi Party away from Hitler and combining it with trade-union support. The strategy failed within four weeks. Strasser was politically broken; Schleicher had no Reichstag majority either; and the trade unions had no reason to trust an aristocratic general.

Meanwhile Papen, furious at being pushed out, was working in private to bring Hitler back into government — with himself as Vice-Chancellor pulling the strings. On 4 January 1933 Papen met Hitler in secret at the Cologne home of the banker Kurt von Schroeder. Industrial donors were lined up to pay off Nazi debts. Within three weeks Schleicher was finished.

The Appointment, 30 January 1933

On 28 January Schleicher resigned. On 29 January Papen presented Hindenburg with his proposed cabinet: Hitler as Chancellor, Papen as Vice-Chancellor and Reich Commissioner for Prussia, Alfred Hugenberg (DNVP) as Economics Minister, and only two other Nazis (Frick and Goring) in the cabinet of eleven. Papen reassured Hindenburg that they had ‘hired’ Hitler and could box him in: ‘Within two months we will have pushed Hitler so far into a corner that he'll squeak.’

Hindenburg, now 85, reluctantly agreed. At noon on 30 January 1933 Hitler was sworn in as Chancellor of Germany. That evening, lit torchlight columns of SA paraded through the Brandenburg Gate. Goebbels wrote in his diary: ‘It is almost like a dream. The Wilhelmstrasse is ours.’ The Nazi share of the cabinet was small — three of eleven — but Hitler had what mattered: control of the Chancellery, command of Reich-level policy, and a President willing to issue Article 48 decrees on his recommendation.

Three layers of cause are usually identified. Structural causes include the Treaty of Versailles, the Article 48 emergency provision, the use of proportional representation that produced fragmented Reichstags, and the survival of anti-democratic elites in the army, judiciary and civil service. Long-term causes include the Depression, the rise of the Nazi and Communist parties, and the discrediting of moderate parties by 1932. Contingent causes are the personal decisions of a small group: Hindenburg's willingness to govern by decree, Papen's vendetta against Schleicher, and the Cologne meeting of 4 January 1933. Hitler's appointment was not inevitable — it was the product of all three layers and an avoidable miscalculation by elite conservatives.

Key Fact

Hitler was appointed, not elected. The Nazis lost 34 seats in November 1932. Hitler became Chancellor on 30 January 1933 because Papen persuaded Hindenburg that a Hitler-led cabinet of three Nazis and eight conservatives could be controlled. Papen's prediction — that they would push Hitler ‘into a corner’ within two months — was the most catastrophic miscalculation in twentieth-century European politics.

lessons.title: The Nazi economy — work, rearmament and self-sufficiency

before.content_html:
When Hitler took power in January 1933 there were six million unemployed Germans. By 1939 official unemployment was under 200,000. Nazi propaganda presented this as a miracle. The reality was more complicated: the figures depended on who was counted, work creation was largely a side-effect of rearmament, and consumers paid for the recovery in lower wages, longer hours and shortages of basic goods. This lesson tracks the Nazi economy from Schacht's New Plan in 1934 to the Four Year Plan of 1936 and the choices behind the slogan ‘guns or butter’.

Schacht's New Plan, 1934

The first phase of recovery was managed by Hjalmar Schacht, a conservative banker who had helped end the 1923 hyperinflation. Schacht became Reichsbank President in March 1933 and Economics Minister in August 1934. His New Plan tackled three problems at once: shortage of foreign exchange, dependence on imports, and mass unemployment.

Schacht imposed strict import controls and signed bilateral trade agreements with Balkan states (Yugoslavia, Romania, Bulgaria), paying for raw materials in blocked Reichsmarks rather than hard currency. He used Mefo bills — promissory notes issued by a shell company — to disguise the true scale of military spending. By 1936 unemployment was down to one million. But Schacht warned Hitler that rearmament was now outrunning what the economy could support without inflation. Hitler was unimpressed.

Key Fact

Official German unemployment fell from six million in 1933 to one million by 1936 and under 200,000 by 1939. The figures are flattering: Jews dismissed under the April 1933 civil service law, women pushed out of professions, political prisoners and the 1.4 million conscripted from 1935 were all redefined out of the count.

Public Works and the Reich Labour Service

Job creation began before Hitler took power, but the Nazis claimed credit and expanded it. The most visible programme was the autobahn network: 7,000 kilometres planned, 3,000 km completed by 1938. Around 125,000 men worked on autobahn construction at peak. Other programmes included public housing, draining marshes, planting forests and building government offices.

From 1935 the RAD (Reichsarbeitsdienst) made six months of labour service compulsory for young men aged 18–25. It paid pocket money rather than a wage, lived under quasi-military discipline, and worked on agricultural drainage, road-building and forestry. From 1939 it was extended to women too. The RAD was a labour scheme, a propaganda spectacle and a pre-conscription training pipeline rolled into one.

In March 1935 Hitler announced conscription in defiance of the Treaty of Versailles, raising the army from 100,000 to 550,000 by 1936. Conscription alone removed roughly 1.4 million young men from the unemployment count. Rearmament also pulled steel, chemicals, coal and engineering firms back into mass production: military spending rose from 1% of GDP in 1933 to around 18% by 1938. Krupp, Thyssen and IG Farben all expanded sharply. The recovery was real for these firms; for consumers it meant their resources were diverted to weapons. The historiographical debate over whether the Nazis ‘solved’ unemployment turns on whether you count conscripts and dismissed Jews and women as employed, unemployed, or simply absent from the figures.

The Four Year Plan, 1936

In August 1936 Hitler issued a secret memorandum demanding that ‘the German army must be operational and the German economy fit for war within four years’. He put Hermann Goring — not Schacht — in charge of a new Four Year Plan. The aim was autarky: economic self-sufficiency that would let Germany fight a war without depending on imports.

The Plan poured investment into synthetic substitutes — synthetic oil from coal, synthetic rubber (Buna), artificial textiles. New plants were built at Leuna and Schkopau. Steel production was forced through new plants at Salzgitter (the Hermann Goring Werke). Imports of consumer goods were squeezed. By 1939 Germany still imported a third of its raw materials. Autarky was a goal, not a reality. But arms production rose sharply: by 1939 Germany was producing 8,000 aircraft a year. Schacht resigned as Economics Minister in November 1937, warning Hitler that the country was running out of foreign exchange.

Strength Through Joy and Beauty of Labour

For workers, the Nazis offered carrots as well as sticks. The German Labour Front (DAF) under Robert Ley ran two flagship organisations. Strength Through Joy (KdF) offered cheap holidays, theatre trips, sports events and concerts. By 1938 ten million Germans had taken a KdF holiday — mostly day trips, but cruises to Madeira and Norway also ran. Beauty of Labour (SdA) improved factory canteens, washrooms and lighting.

The famous KdF promise was the Volkswagen — the ‘people's car’ that workers could buy through a savings scheme launched in 1938. Roughly 336,000 Germans paid in. Not one civilian Volkswagen was delivered before 1945; the factory was switched to making the Kubelwagen for the army. Like much of Nazi welfare, KdF combined real benefits, real propaganda value and an undertow of state fraud.

Drawbacks for Workers and Consumers

Behind the propaganda, ordinary German workers paid in three currencies. First, real wages fell or stagnated for most of the 1930s — not until 1938 did average industrial wages match 1928 levels. The DAF set wages; strikes were illegal; workbooks restricted job changes from 1935. Second, the working week lengthened — from 43 hours in 1933 to over 49 by 1939, with bonus pay for overtime gradually eroded. Third, consumer goods were rationed in all but name — meat, butter, dairy and textiles were all in short supply by 1939 because resources had gone into arms.

Goring put the choice plainly in 1936: ‘Guns will make us powerful; butter will only make us fat.’ The Nazi economy delivered on guns. It did not deliver on butter.

Two competing answers. The official answer is yes — six million in 1933 to under 200,000 in 1939. The qualified answer is partial — subtract roughly 1.4 million conscripts, perhaps half a million Jews dismissed under the April 1933 law, women redefined out of full-time work, and political prisoners in the camps, and the figure of true productive employment is much smaller. Historians of the Nazi economy (Tooze; Overy) generally accept the recovery was real but driven by rearmament rather than productive demand — an ‘armaments boom’ that could only end in war or collapse.

Key Fact

By 1938 around 18% of German GDP went to the military, up from 1% in 1933. Average industrial wages did not match 1928 levels until 1938, the working week stretched to over 49 hours, and consumer goods were rationed in all but name. The economy worked — for armaments. It did not work for consumers.

lessons.title: Nazi social policy — women, youth, churches

before.content_html:
The Nazi state did not stop at controlling parliament, the police and the economy. It set out to remake the German family, the German classroom and the German pulpit. Women, young people and churches were each redirected towards Volksgemeinschaft — the racial national community. This lesson tracks how policy targeted each group, what it achieved, and where it ran into resistance.

Women: Kinder, Kuche, Kirche

Nazi ideology assigned women a single primary role: bearing and raising racially-pure German children. The slogan was Kinder, Kuche, Kirche — children, kitchen, church. The 1933 Law for the Encouragement of Marriage offered interest-free loans of 1,000 marks to newly-wed couples on condition that the wife left work; one quarter of the loan was written off for each child born. Around 800,000 loans were taken up by 1937.

Birth-rate incentives followed. The Mother's Cross was instituted in 1938: bronze for four children, silver for six, gold for eight. Women in ‘racially-valuable’ categories were honoured publicly. The Lebensborn programme, run by Himmler from 1936, set up SS-controlled maternity homes where unmarried women deemed racially ‘valuable’ could give birth secretly to children fathered by SS men. Women were squeezed out of the professions: by 1934 the number of female teachers, doctors and civil servants had been cut sharply. Married women were taxed more heavily on second incomes.

Key Fact

Nazi ideology defined women's role as Kinder, Kuche, Kirche. The 1933 Marriage Loans, the 1938 Mother's Cross and Himmler's Lebensborn homes all targeted the birth rate. By 1939, however, war labour shortages had forced the regime to push women back into factories, contradicting its own propaganda.

Women: From Hearth to Wartime Factory

The Three Ks ran into the iron rules of arithmetic. Rearmament from 1935 created a labour shortage that could not be filled by men alone. From 1937 women were quietly encouraged back into work; by 1939 there were more women in employment than in 1933. From 1939 the RAD (Reich Labour Service) was extended to women. By 1944 around 14 million German women worked. The Nazi message remained traditional but the practice was contradictory: women were both honoured as mothers and conscripted as workers.

It depends which woman. Working-class women already in factories saw little material change. Professional women lost most: female lawyers, judges and university teachers were excluded under early laws. Married rural women may have welcomed marriage loans and child subsidies. Jewish women lost their citizenship rights under the 1935 Nuremberg Laws and were excluded from welfare entirely. Women in the BDM gained subsidised travel, sport and a peer group, but lost the chance to enter male-dominated professions. Avoid the blanket statement ‘Nazi policy banned women from work’ — the picture is uneven and changes between 1933 and 1944.

Hitler Youth and the BDM

Nazi youth policy aimed to capture every German child between 10 and 18. The Hitler Youth (HJ) took boys from 14 to 18; the Jungvolk took boys from 10 to 14; the BDM (Bund Deutscher Madel) took girls from 14 to 18, with the Jungmadel for younger girls. Membership grew from 100,000 in 1933 to 8.5 million by 1939.

Activity for boys was paramilitary: marching, weapons handling, map-reading, camping. Activity for girls was domestic and physical: gymnastics, cooking, child-care, racial-purity instruction. All members swore an oath of personal loyalty to Hitler. The 1936 Hitler Youth Law made the HJ the only legal youth organisation. The 1939 Youth Service Law made membership compulsory for all German children of relevant age. Older youth groups — Catholic, Protestant, scout — were disbanded or absorbed.

Education and the Curriculum

Schools were brought into line under Bernhard Rust as Reich Education Minister from 1934. Textbooks were rewritten. Maths problems calculated the cost of disabled people to the state or the trajectory of artillery shells. Biology became racial hygiene: skull measurement, Aryan superiority, the dangers of mixed marriage. PE rose to fifteen periods a week to build soldiers and mothers. Jewish teachers and pupils were excluded under the 1933 Civil Service Law and the 1938 expulsion of Jewish children. Classroom prayers were replaced with Nazi morning songs in many schools.

For elite training, three school networks were set up. Napola schools (National Political Educational Institutions) trained future SS officers and civil servants. Adolf Hitler Schools, controlled by the Hitler Youth, trained party administrators. Ordensburgen castles trained the senior cadre of the future Reich. Universities were also brought into line: 15% of teaching staff were dismissed by 1934, and student membership of Nazi organisations became effectively compulsory.

Most German children passed through HJ or BDM and a Nazified curriculum, but reception was uneven. Younger children absorbed the propaganda most thoroughly — they had no comparison. Older boys often complained that the HJ was repetitive and bullying; the Edelweiss Pirates and Swing Youth (covered in lesson 14) were partly a response. Catholic and Confessional Church families resisted in pockets. After the war, oral histories collected by historians like Detlev Peukert showed that hostility to the regime grew especially after 1942 as casualty figures rose. Indoctrination was wide but not always deep.

Churches: The Concordat and the Reich Church

Hitler had to manage Germany's two main Christian denominations: roughly 22 million Catholics and 40 million Protestants. With the Catholic Church he signed the Concordat on 20 July 1933 — the Vatican accepted political non-interference in exchange for protection of Catholic schools and lay organisations. The deal gave Hitler international respectability and removed the Centre Party as a political force. Within months the regime had begun violating its terms by attacking Catholic youth groups and lay associations.

For Protestants, the regime created the Reich Church under Ludwig Muller in 1933. The Reich Church merged regional Lutheran churches under Nazi influence, removed the Old Testament from teaching where possible (because of its Jewish origins), and tried to introduce a Nazified version of Christianity. Crosses were replaced with swastikas in some Reich Church services.

The Confessional Church and Resistance

A breakaway group of Protestant pastors refused to accept the Reich Church. They formed the Confessional Church in 1934, led initially by Martin Niemoller. The Barmen Declaration of May 1934 rejected the Nazi claim that the church should serve the state. Roughly 6,000 pastors signed up. Niemoller was arrested in 1937 and held in concentration camps until 1945. Dietrich Bonhoeffer joined the resistance and was executed in April 1945. Pope Pius XI's encyclical Mit brennender Sorge of March 1937 condemned Nazi racial ideology — smuggled into Germany and read from Catholic pulpits on Palm Sunday.

By 1939 the regime had not destroyed the churches but had not converted them either. Most Germans went on attending Sunday services. The state had infiltrated the leadership but failed to win the pews.

Key Fact

The Concordat (July 1933) bought Catholic neutrality but was quickly broken. The Reich Church (1933) failed to absorb the Confessional Church (1934). The Hitler Youth Law (1936) made the HJ the only legal youth movement. The Youth Service Law (1939) made membership compulsory. Each step extended Nazi control of social life, but resistance from the churches and the white-flight of older youth showed it never reached every German home.

Hitler Youth — main Nazi youth organisation for boys aged 14–18 (Jungvolk for younger boys); compulsory by stages from 1936, with paramilitary training and ideological indoctrination.
League of German Maidens — the female branch of the Hitler Youth from 1930; took girls 14–18, with sport, camping and a curriculum of motherhood and racial purity.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1939 BDM publication celebrating young women's loyalty to the Volksgemeinschaft) and Interpretation B (a 1980s oral history of women born in the 1920s arguing the regime's traditional rhetoric collided with wartime factory work) on Nazi policy towards women. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents Nazi women's policy as a unified ideology — motherhood, sport and racial pride.
• Interpretation B presents the policy as contradictory in practice — women were honoured at home and conscripted into factories.
• Main difference: A frames the policy as ideologically coherent; B frames it as practically contradictory.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1939 BDM publication) and Interpretation B (a 1980s oral history) give different views about Nazi policy towards women.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They had different purposes — the 1939 publication aimed to mobilise consent for Nazi gender ideology; the oral history aimed to collect lived experience.
• They drew on different evidence — the publication used model BDM members; the oral history used elderly women's memories of marriage, factory work and rationing.
• They were produced under different conditions — the 1939 source was censored Nazi propaganda; the oral history had post-war freedom to disagree with regime ideology.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: 'The Hitler Youth and BDM successfully turned a generation of Germans into committed Nazis by 1939.' To what extent is Interpretation A convincing about the impact of Nazi youth policy?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because membership rose from 100,000 in 1933 to 8.5 million by 1939; the 1936 Hitler Youth Law and 1939 Youth Service Law made membership effectively universal.
• Convincing because schools were brought into line under Rust, with racial hygiene compulsory and elite Napola/Adolf Hitler Schools trained the future cadre.
• Less convincing because alternative youth groups — Edelweiss Pirates, Swing Youth — existed in working-class and middle-class areas precisely because the HJ was unpopular with some young people.
• Less convincing because oral histories show older boys often resented the HJ as bullying and repetitive; younger children absorbed propaganda more deeply than teenagers.
• Less convincing because Catholic and Confessional Church families maintained alternative loyalties through Sunday school and family practice.
• Overall judgement: Nazi youth policy reached almost every German child by 1939 but its depth varied with age, region, family background and date — reach was high, conversion uneven.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Nazi religious policy on the German churches between 1933 and 1939.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The Concordat of 20 July 1933 bought Catholic neutrality and removed the Centre Party from politics — but its terms were broken within months as Catholic youth groups were attacked.
• The Reich Church was created in 1933 under Ludwig Muller to absorb Protestant churches — but failed to capture all pastors, prompting the breakaway Confessional Church (Barmen Declaration, 1934).
• Resistance grew — Niemoller was imprisoned in 1937; Pope Pius XI's encyclical Mit brennender Sorge (March 1937) condemned Nazi racial ideology and was read from Catholic pulpits.
• Sunday attendance largely held up — the regime infiltrated leadership but did not capture lay believers, demonstrating the limits of Nazi totalitarian reach.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific dates. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of Nazi social policy and its impact on Germans.
You may consider:
• policies aimed at women and young people
• policies aimed at the Christian churches.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Women: Three Ks slogan; Marriage Loans 1933; Mother's Cross 1938; Lebensborn 1936; exclusion from professions early on; from 1937 push back into factories; RAD extended to women in 1939; 14 million working by 1944.
• Young people: Hitler Youth Law 1936; Youth Service Law 1939; HJ membership 100,000 (1933) to 8.5 million (1939); Napola and Adolf Hitler Schools; rewritten curriculum under Rust; PE up to 15 periods; racial hygiene compulsory.
• Churches: Concordat July 1933; Reich Church under Muller; Confessional Church 1934 with Barmen Declaration; Niemoller imprisoned 1937; Bonhoeffer executed 1945; Mit brennender Sorge encyclical 1937.
• Limits: women contradiction between motherhood and factory work; Edelweiss Pirates and Swing Youth as alternatives; church resistance from Confessional and Catholic clergy.
• Conclusion: Nazi social policy reached every major institution — family, school and pulpit — but its depth was uneven. Indoctrination was strongest with younger children; weakest with older boys, professional women and committed Christians. The regime infiltrated leadership but rarely captured private conviction.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1937 Nazi propaganda film celebrating the Hitler Youth as the future of Germany) and Interpretation B (a Confessional Church sermon arguing the regime was capturing children from their parents) on Nazi youth policy. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the HJ as a national triumph — comradeship, sport and loyalty to Hitler.
• Interpretation B presents the HJ as a threat to family and faith — an attempt to displace Christian upbringing.
• Main difference: A celebrates state youth policy; B sees it as competition with family and church.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

lessons.title: Aryan ideas, racial policy and the Final Solution

before.content_html:
This lesson covers the most painful subject on the AQA spec: the Nazi regime's persecution and murder of millions of European Jews, alongside Sinti and Roma, disabled Germans, gay men, Soviet prisoners and political opponents. The historical task is to track the radicalisation step by step — from the boycott of April 1933 to the death camps from 1942 — and to ask the question that still divides historians: was the Holocaust a long-held plan that Hitler put into action, or a process that radicalised in stages as the regime found itself in war?

Nazi Racial Ideology

Nazi ideology divided humanity into hierarchies of race. At the top was the imagined Aryan race — tall, fair-haired, blue-eyed Germans. Below them came other Europeans, then Slavs, with Jews, Sinti and Roma, and black Africans placed at the bottom as Untermenschen — sub-humans. This had no scientific basis. It was social Darwinism plus pseudo-anthropology, taught in German schools as racial hygiene from 1935. The ideology was not invented by Hitler — antisemitism had a long European history — but the Nazi state mechanised it.

Mendelian skull measurement, eye colour charts and family-tree research were marshalled to classify Germans as fully Jewish, half-Jewish or quarter-Jewish (Mischling). What followed was not yet murder, but it built the legal infrastructure that would make organised killing possible.

Key Fact

Nazi racial policy moved through clear stages: boycotts and dismissals from 1933, legal exclusion under the Nuremberg Laws (September 1935), organised violence at Kristallnacht (November 1938), mass shootings by the Einsatzgruppen from 1941, and industrial murder coordinated from the Wannsee Conference (January 1942). The radicalisation was not one decision but a sequence.

Persecution 1933–38

Persecution began within weeks of Hitler's appointment. On 1 April 1933 SA squads enforced a national boycott of Jewish businesses, painting Stars of David and the word Jude on shop windows. The Civil Service Law of 7 April 1933 dismissed Jewish judges, teachers, doctors and academics from the public payroll. Quotas restricted Jewish students at universities and Jewish patients in hospitals.

In September 1935 the Reichstag passed the Nuremberg Laws. The Reich Citizenship Law stripped German Jews of citizenship; only those of German or Aryan blood could be Reich citizens. The Law for the Protection of German Blood banned marriage and sexual relations between Jews and non-Jews. Sinti and Roma were soon classed under the same provisions. By 1938 around half of Germany's 500,000 Jews had emigrated — the others lacked the visas, money or contacts to leave.

On 7 November 1938 a young Polish Jew, Herschel Grynszpan, shot a German diplomat in Paris in protest at the deportation of his parents. Goebbels seized on the killing to authorise a coordinated wave of state-organised violence. Across Germany and Austria on the night of 9–10 November 1938, SA and SS units (some in plainclothes) attacked Jewish synagogues, businesses and homes. Around 267 synagogues were burned. Around 7,500 Jewish-owned businesses were ransacked or destroyed. At least 91 Jews were murdered. About 30,000 Jewish men were arrested and sent to concentration camps. The community was then fined one billion marks for ‘causing’ the disorder. Kristallnacht was the moment Nazi antisemitism moved from social and legal persecution to organised state violence in public — with no significant German protest.

The T4 Programme and Other Victims

In October 1939 (backdated to 1 September) Hitler signed an order authorising what became known as the T4 programme — the murder of disabled Germans deemed ‘unworthy of life’. Around 70,000 people were killed by gas, lethal injection or starvation in six killing centres including Hadamar and Hartheim before the official programme was halted in August 1941 after a sermon by Bishop Galen of Munster. Killings of disabled people in fact continued informally to 1945.

Other groups were targeted alongside Jews: Sinti and Roma (around 220,000 to 500,000 murdered), gay men (around 50,000 imprisoned, perhaps 15,000 sent to camps), Soviet prisoners of war (around 3.3 million dead in German captivity), Polish elites (mass murders from 1939), and political opponents. The Holocaust is centrally about the murder of European Jews; it was not only the murder of European Jews. Reducing it to a single number or a single victim group is historically inaccurate.

From Persecution to Mass Killing, 1939–41

War transformed the policy. From September 1939 millions of Polish Jews came under German occupation. They were forced into ghettos — sealed urban districts in Warsaw, Lodz, Cracow and elsewhere — with starvation rations and forced labour. Around 100,000 died of disease and hunger in the Warsaw ghetto in 1941–42 alone.

From June 1941, with the invasion of the Soviet Union (Operation Barbarossa), Einsatzgruppen (SS mobile killing units) followed the German army into Soviet territory. They murdered around 1.3 to 1.5 million Jews, communist officials and others by mass shooting. At Babi Yar, near Kiev, around 33,771 Jews were shot in two days (29–30 September 1941) on the regime's own count. The killers were ordinary German police, SS, Wehrmacht support and local collaborators.

The Wannsee Conference and the Death Camps

On 20 January 1942 fifteen senior officials — including Reinhard Heydrich (chair), Adolf Eichmann (secretary) and representatives of the Foreign Office, Justice Ministry and SS — met in a villa at Wannsee in suburban Berlin. The minutes — one of the few surviving copies — coordinated the Final Solution: the systematic deportation and murder of all 11 million European Jews, including Jews in countries Germany did not yet occupy.

Wannsee did not start the killing. Mass shootings had been under way since June 1941. Gas vans had been used at Chelmno from December 1941. What Wannsee did was bureaucratically coordinate the murder across the Nazi state and align deportations from Western Europe with the killing centres being built in occupied Poland. From 1942 onwards Jewish communities were transported by train to six dedicated death camps: Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, Sobibor, Belzec, Chelmno and Majdanek. Roughly six million Jews were murdered by 1945 — about two thirds of pre-war European Jewry.

These are not the same and the difference matters in exam answers. Concentration camps (Konzentrationslager) such as Dachau (opened 1933), Buchenwald (1937) and Sachsenhausen (1936) held political prisoners, religious minorities, Roma, gay men and Jews; deaths were from forced labour, malnutrition, disease and execution. Death camps (Vernichtungslager) such as Treblinka, Sobibor, Belzec and Chelmno were built from 1941–42 with the sole purpose of industrial murder, almost entirely of Jews. Auschwitz-Birkenau and Majdanek combined both functions. Conflating them flattens the historical record.

Intentionalists and Functionalists

Historians have debated for decades how this happened. Intentionalists (Lucy Dawidowicz, Klaus Hildebrand, Daniel Goldhagen) argue Hitler held a consistent plan for racial extermination from at least 1925 and the Holocaust was the deliberate execution of that plan. Functionalists (Hans Mommsen, Christopher Browning, Raul Hilberg) argue the killing radicalised step by step as the regime confronted millions of Jews under occupation, with mid-level officials proposing increasingly murderous solutions. Most historians today take a moderate position: Hitler's antisemitism was a constant; the specific decision for industrial murder emerged in 1941–42 from the dynamics of war and occupation, not from a 1925 master plan. Naming named victims and named perpetrators — rather than abstract numbers — is the historical practice both schools agree on.

Key Fact

Around six million Jews were murdered in the Holocaust, alongside Sinti and Roma, disabled Germans (T4), gay men, Soviet POWs and political prisoners. The radicalisation moved from boycotts (1933) to legal exclusion (1935), state violence (1938), ghettoisation (from 1939), mass shooting (from 1941) and industrial murder coordinated at Wannsee (1942). Most historians now reject a single 1925 plan in favour of stepped radicalisation under wartime conditions.

lessons.title: Propaganda, the police state and Nazi culture

before.content_html:
If the Enabling Act made the Nazi state legal and Gleichschaltung made it ubiquitous, propaganda and the police state made it stick. Joseph Goebbels controlled what most Germans heard, read and watched. Heinrich Himmler controlled what they feared. Between them they shaped a public sphere in which loyalty was constant, dissent was costly and the line between consent and coercion blurred. This lesson tracks how the Nazi regime used propaganda, censorship, culture and terror to hold a population of 67 million.

Goebbels and the Ministry of Propaganda

In March 1933 Hitler created a new Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda for Joseph Goebbels. Within months the ministry controlled press, radio, film, theatre, music, literature and art through a Reich Chamber of Culture. Journalists, actors, writers and musicians had to be members; non-Aryans and political opponents were excluded. Goebbels held a daily press briefing telling editors what to print and what to avoid.

The propaganda message had a small core: Hitler as saviour, the Volk as racial community, the Versailles ‘stab in the back’ as the wound to be reversed, Communism and Jewry as the threats. Repetition mattered. So did variety: Goebbels promoted not only mass rallies but film comedies, sports broadcasts and cookery columns. Most German entertainment under the Nazis was non-political; it just made the regime seem normal.

Key Fact

By 1939 around 70% of German households owned a Volksempfanger receiver — the highest radio ownership in the world. Goebbels controlled radio output through a single state broadcaster; loudspeakers in factories, offices and public squares broadcast Hitler's speeches to those without sets. Radio was the regime's most powerful single propaganda tool.

Tools: Radio, Film, Press, Posters, Rallies

The Volksempfanger (‘people's receiver’) was a deliberately cheap radio sold from 1933 with a tuning range limited to German stations. The regime sold around 12 million by 1939. In factories, restaurants and squares loudspeaker pillars carried Hitler's speeches into shared space. Radio neutralised foreign broadcasting (BBC German service) for most ordinary Germans, while delivering ministerial messages to the kitchen and the workshop.

Film was the second pillar. Triumph of the Will (1935), filmed by Leni Riefenstahl at the 1934 Nuremberg rally, set a new standard for political cinema with moving cameras, aerial footage and choreographed crowd shots. Olympia (1938) did the same with the 1936 Berlin Games. Most cinema output, however, was light entertainment with subtle ideological framing — comedies, melodramas, costume pictures — bookended by official newsreels (the Wochenschau) covering battles, rallies and Hitler's appearances.

Press output was concentrated in the party-controlled Volkischer Beobachter and a network of regional dailies. Independent papers were squeezed out: by 1939 around two thirds of German papers were either owned by the party or published under its direction. Posters by artists like Hans Schweitzer (‘Mjolnir’) saturated public space with iconography of soldier-hero, family, Volk and Fuhrer. Mass rallies — Nuremberg every September from 1933 — staged the regime as religious ritual: torchlight, eagle insignia, mass salutes, choreographed columns.

The 1936 Berlin Olympics

The August 1936 Berlin Olympics was the regime's largest single propaganda spectacle. New stadia, the Olympic Village, the first televised Games and a tightly orchestrated reception of foreign visitors presented Nazi Germany as orderly, modern and racially confident. Antisemitic posters were temporarily removed from Berlin streets. The Games were a public-relations triumph in much of the foreign press — even though the African-American athlete Jesse Owens won four gold medals against the regime's racial doctrine. Most foreign visitors went home with a flattering image of the regime, which was the point.

On 10 May 1933, four months after Hitler took power, students orchestrated by the Nazi Student Association burned around 25,000 books outside the State Opera House in Berlin and across other university towns. Targets included works by Jewish authors (Stefan Zweig, Albert Einstein), pacifists (Erich Maria Remarque), socialists (Karl Marx) and modernists (Thomas Mann, Bertolt Brecht). The poet Heinrich Heine had warned a century earlier that ‘wherever they burn books, in the end they will also burn human beings.’ Censorship continued through the Reich Chamber of Culture's exclusion of non-Aryan and politically suspect writers; the 1937 ‘Degenerate Art’ exhibition mocked modernist painters Paul Klee, Otto Dix and Max Beckmann while praising Aryan-realist artists alongside.

Nazi Culture: Blood and Soil

The official cultural ideal was ‘blood-and-soil’ (Blut und Boden) realism: paintings of farmers, Aryan mothers and soldiers; sculpture of muscular nudes by Arno Breker; folk music and Wagner. Modernism was banned. The 1937 Degenerate Art exhibition in Munich displayed roughly 650 confiscated modern works as warnings; it drew over two million visitors, possibly the largest modern art exhibition of the century. Architecture was monumental: Albert Speer's plans for Berlin (the ‘Welthauptstadt Germania’) and the Zeppelin Field at Nuremberg used scale to dwarf the individual citizen and elevate the regime.

The Police State: Himmler, the SS and the Gestapo

The other half of control was fear. Heinrich Himmler ran the SS (Schutzstaffel) from 1929 and from 1936 controlled the unified Reich police. The SS grew from a personal bodyguard of around 200 to a state-within-the-state of around 240,000 by 1939. It ran the concentration camp system from 1934, the Einsatzgruppen from 1941 and the Waffen-SS combat divisions during the war.

The Gestapo (Geheime Staatspolizei) had around 32,000 officers across all of Germany by 1944 — far smaller than its reputation. It depended on civilian denunciation. Block wardens (Blockwarte) reported on apartment buildings; informers reported on workplaces; ex-SPD and KPD members were watched closely. Roughly 80% of Gestapo investigations originated in tips from ordinary Germans, not from independent surveillance. Concentration camps held around 25,000 inmates by 1939, mainly political prisoners, religious minorities, Jews and gay men. The People's Court (Volksgerichtshof, 1934) handed down political death sentences with no appeal.

Examiner reports flag the conflation regularly. The SA was the brown-shirted street paramilitary of the 1920s and early 1930s, broken in the Night of the Long Knives in June 1934. The SS was Himmler's elite black-uniformed organisation, expanding from 1934 to control camps, secret police and (from 1941) Einsatzgruppen. The Gestapo was the Nazi secret state police, founded by Goring in Prussia in April 1933 and brought under Himmler in 1934. Different bodies, different uniforms, different roles. Lock the distinction in.

Self-Policing and the Limits of Control

The most powerful police mechanism was self-policing. Most Germans never met a Gestapo officer; they policed their conversations because they did not know who else might be listening. Nazi sociologists called this the ‘atomisation’ of public life. Yet the regime never achieved total control. Older workers told private jokes about Goring's medals. Catholic and Confessional Church congregations maintained an alternative moral world. Foreign radio (the BBC's German service from 1938) was illegal but listened to. Edelweiss Pirates and Swing Youth (covered in lesson 14) found subcultural escape. Propaganda saturation was high; conviction was uneven; private dissent persisted in pockets even before the war turned against Germany.

Key Fact

The Gestapo had only around 32,000 officers across the entire Reich by 1944 but felt larger because Germans informed on neighbours. Roughly 80% of Gestapo investigations began with a civilian tip. Terror operated through self-policing as much as state surveillance — an important historiographical correction to the Hollywood image of an omniscient secret police.

lessons.title: Opposition, resistance and Germany at war

before.content_html:
By 1939 the Nazi state had reshaped almost every German institution. Yet there were always Germans who refused to be reshaped. This final lesson covers two linked topics on the AQA spec: the opposition and resistance to Nazi rule, and the impact of war on the homefront. It also asks the question that examiners reward most in 12-mark essays: did opposition matter, given that it failed to remove Hitler? Significance is not the same as effectiveness.

Forms of Opposition

Opposition under the Third Reich ran through five rough categories. Private grumbling: jokes, foreign-radio listening, refusing to give the Nazi salute. Subcultural resistance: youth movements like Edelweiss Pirates and Swing Youth that rejected Hitler Youth norms. Religious resistance: the Confessional Church, Catholic clergy, Bishop Galen's 1941 sermon against T4. Political resistance: KPD and SPD networks operating underground. Conservative-military resistance: senior officers and civil servants who came to plot Hitler's removal. None of these toppled the regime; together they show consent was never universal.

Key Fact

Opposition took five forms: private grumbling, youth subcultures (Edelweiss Pirates, Swing Youth), religious resistance (Niemoller, Bonhoeffer, Galen), political networks (underground KPD and SPD) and conservative-military plotting (Beck, Stauffenberg). The regime treated all five as treason — tens of thousands were imprisoned or executed by 1945.

Swing Youth

In Hamburg, Berlin and other cities, mostly middle-class teenagers from 1939 onwards rejected Nazi cultural norms by listening to American and British Swing jazz, dancing in mixed-sex couples, growing their hair long and dressing in Anglophile fashions. Around 6,000 people attended a Swing festival in Hamburg in 1940. The Swing Youth were not political in any organised sense, but they refused the Hitler Youth's choreographed culture. From 1940 the Gestapo arrested Swing Youth leaders; some were sent to camps and forced to wear shaved heads as humiliation.

Edelweiss Pirates

In the Ruhr and Cologne working-class districts, the Edelweiss Pirates formed informal gangs from the late 1930s. They wore the Edelweiss flower badge, sang anti-Nazi versions of folk songs, and physically attacked Hitler Youth patrols. During the war they distributed Allied propaganda leaflets. In Cologne the local Edelweiss Pirates sheltered deserters, escaped slave labourers and Allied airmen; in November 1944 they helped to assassinate the local Gestapo chief, and twelve pirates were publicly hanged in retaliation. The Edelweiss Pirates were a class-based protest movement as well as a generational one.

The White Rose

In Munich, a small group of university students and one professor formed the White Rose in 1942. Hans and Sophie Scholl, with their philosophy professor Kurt Huber and friends Christoph Probst, Alexander Schmorell and Willi Graf, produced six leaflets denouncing Nazi murder of Jews and disabled people. The leaflets were duplicated by hand and posted to addresses across Germany. On 18 February 1943 Sophie was caught throwing leaflets from a balcony at the University of Munich. Four days later she, Hans and Probst were sentenced to death by the People's Court and executed by guillotine. Huber and the others followed. The fifth leaflet was smuggled out of Germany and dropped over the country by Allied aircraft — making it the only Nazi-era resistance text to reach a mass German audience during the war.

Niemoller's Confessional Church kept independent Protestant theology alive; Niemoller himself was held in Sachsenhausen and Dachau from 1937 to 1945. Bishop Clemens August von Galen of Munster delivered a sermon in August 1941 publicly denouncing the T4 euthanasia killings; the regime suspended the official programme weeks later, although informal killings of disabled people continued. Dietrich Bonhoeffer joined the conservative resistance from his Confessional Church base, smuggling intelligence to Britain through the Abwehr. He was arrested in April 1943 and hanged at Flossenburg on 9 April 1945, weeks before the regime's collapse.

The July 1944 Bomb Plot

By 1943 a circle of conservative officers and civil servants had concluded that only Hitler's death could end the war. Their leader was Colonel Claus von Stauffenberg, a Wehrmacht staff officer wounded in North Africa. Their plan, Operation Valkyrie, used a contingency plan for the Reserve Army to take over Berlin in case of an SS uprising — subverting it for a coup against Hitler.

On 20 July 1944 Stauffenberg attended a briefing at Hitler's eastern headquarters, the Wolf's Lair in Rastenburg. He left a briefcase containing a primed bomb under the table and excused himself. The bomb exploded at 12:42 p.m. but the briefcase had been moved behind a heavy oak table support; four officers were killed but Hitler suffered only minor injuries. In Berlin, conspirators believed Hitler dead and began arrests under Operation Valkyrie. By evening the news was clear that Hitler had survived. Stauffenberg, General Ludwig Beck and three others were arrested and shot in the courtyard of the Bendlerblock that night. Around 200 conspirators were executed in the following months. Some were hanged with piano wire from meat hooks at Plotzensee Prison; films of the executions were shown to Hitler. Around 5,000 people connected to the plot or its sympathisers were eventually arrested.

The Wartime Economy and Speer

War transformed the German economy. Albert Speer, appointed Reich Minister for Armaments in February 1942, rationalised arms production: tank output rose from 4,200 in 1941 to 19,000 in 1944, despite Allied bombing. The price was paid by foreign labour. By 1944 around 7.5 million foreign workers (Polish, Russian, French) were forced to work in German factories — a quarter of the total workforce. They were housed in barracks, paid little or nothing, and often worked under starvation rations.

On 18 February 1943, after Stalingrad, Goebbels gave his ‘total war’ speech in the Berlin Sportpalast, calling for the full mobilisation of German society for war production. Cinemas, restaurants and luxury shops were closed; non-essential consumer goods stopped being made. Women aged 17 to 45 were required to register for war work. Rationing tightened: bread rations fell from 2,400g per week in 1939 to 1,700g by 1945; meat from 700g to 250g; fat from 270g to 80g.

From 1942 the RAF's Bomber Command and from 1943 the US Eighth Air Force conducted area bombing of German cities. Hamburg in July 1943 (Operation Gomorrah) suffered a firestorm that killed around 37,000 people in one week. Berlin endured a sustained Bomber Command campaign from November 1943. Dresden was destroyed on 13–15 February 1945 with around 25,000 deaths in two nights. By 1945 around 600,000 German civilians had died in Allied bombing, and 7.5 million were homeless. Whether area bombing was militarily decisive or morally justified remains historically contested; what is not disputed is that it transformed daily civilian life from 1943 onwards.

Refugee Crisis 1944–45

From summer 1944 the Eastern Front collapsed. As the Red Army advanced, around 12 million ethnic Germans fled westward from East Prussia, Pomerania and Silesia. Many died in the bitter winter of 1944–45. The Wilhelm Gustloff, a former cruise ship evacuating refugees from Gdynia, was sunk by a Soviet submarine in January 1945 with the loss of around 9,000 lives — the worst single maritime disaster in history. By May 1945 most of eastern Germany had been emptied of its civilian population, and the Soviet zone of occupation absorbed the surviving refugees alongside its own military operations.

Did Opposition Matter?

No internal opposition removed Hitler — the regime collapsed because Allied armies entered Berlin. But significance is not the same as effectiveness. The Edelweiss Pirates and White Rose preserved the idea that Germans could resist; Galen's sermon halted the official T4 programme; Niemoller and Bonhoeffer kept Christian dissent alive; Stauffenberg's bomb showed even at the heart of the Wehrmacht the regime was opposed. After 1945 these stories shaped how post-war Germany understood its responsibility — the Federal Republic adopted Stauffenberg's Bendlerblock as a memorial. Opposition mattered because it preserved an alternative Germany inside the Third Reich, even though it could not bring the Reich down.

Key Fact

Stauffenberg's bomb at the Wolf's Lair on 20 July 1944 killed four officers but only wounded Hitler. Stauffenberg, Beck and three others were shot at the Bendlerblock the same night; around 5,000 conspirators or sympathisers were eventually arrested. The plot failed in its immediate aim but proved that resistance reached the highest levels of the German military.

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1944 Nazi People's Court verdict denouncing the July 1944 plotters as a small clique of cowards) and Interpretation B (a 1960s West German memorial study presenting the plotters as patriotic martyrs whose action preserved an alternative Germany) on the July 1944 bomb plot. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A presents the plotters as treasonous — isolated, self-interested and contemptible.
• Interpretation B presents the plotters as patriotic — representative of an alternative Germany willing to risk death to end the war.
• Main difference: A frames the plot as criminal failure; B frames it as morally and politically significant resistance.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]

practice_questions.text: Suggest one reason why Interpretation A (a 1944 People's Court verdict) and Interpretation B (a 1960s West German memorial study) give different views about the July 1944 bomb plot.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They were written for different purposes — the People's Court verdict aimed to legitimise mass executions; the memorial study aimed to construct a usable post-war German identity.
• They drew on different evidence — the verdict used selective interrogation transcripts; the memorial study used surviving conspirators' testimony, family papers and archival access.
• They were written under different political conditions — the verdict under regime control with no possibility of dissent; the memorial study under the Federal Republic, which adopted the Bendlerblock as official memorial.
[Mastering (4): one developed reason explained with reference to evidence/purpose/time. Secure (3): one clear reason with limited explanation. Developing (2): identifies a reason but does not explain it. Emerging (1): describes the views again.]

practice_questions.text: Read Interpretation A: 'German opposition to the Nazi regime was insignificant because it failed to remove Hitler.' To what extent is Interpretation A convincing about resistance under the Third Reich?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Convincing because no internal opposition toppled the regime — Stauffenberg's bomb on 20 July 1944 failed; Hitler survived; around 5,000 conspirators were eventually arrested.
• Convincing because youth groups (Swing Youth, Edelweiss Pirates) and the White Rose were small in number and easily crushed.
• Less convincing because Galen's August 1941 sermon halted the official T4 programme — opposition could change policy.
• Less convincing because the White Rose's fifth leaflet was smuggled to Britain and dropped over Germany by Allied aircraft — it reached a mass audience.
• Less convincing because significance is not the same as effectiveness — Niemoller, Bonhoeffer, Stauffenberg and the Scholls preserved an alternative Germany that shaped post-war identity.
• Overall judgement: opposition did not topple the regime but it changed specific policies (T4) and preserved a moral alternative that was decisive in shaping the post-1945 Federal Republic. To dismiss it as ‘insignificant’ conflates effectiveness with significance.
[Mastering (7-8): integrates wording of interpretation, specific contextual knowledge, substantiated judgement. Secure (5-6): contextual evaluation with limited integration. Developing (3-4): paraphrases or context only. Emerging (1-2): generic description.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the war on the German civilian population between 1939 and 1945.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Total-war mobilisation from February 1943 closed cinemas, restaurants and luxury shops; women aged 17 to 45 were required to register for war work; rationing tightened (bread, meat, fat).
• Allied bombing killed around 600,000 German civilians by 1945 and made 7.5 million homeless — Hamburg's firestorm (July 1943) killed around 37,000 in a week; Dresden's destruction (February 1945) killed around 25,000 in two nights.
• Forced labour from across occupied Europe — around 7.5 million foreign workers in German factories by 1944, a quarter of the workforce, often housed in barracks under starvation rations.
• Refugee crisis — around 12 million ethnic Germans fled westward from the eastern provinces in winter 1944–45; the sinking of the Wilhelm Gustloff in January 1945 cost around 9,000 lives.
[Mastering (7-8): two or more developed effects with specific figures. Secure (5-6): two effects with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two underdeveloped. Emerging (1-2): identifies an effect without explanation.]

practice_questions.text:
Construct an explanation of opposition to Nazi rule in Germany between 1933 and 1945.
You may consider:
• youth, religious and student opposition
• conservative and military resistance, including the July 1944 bomb plot.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Youth subcultures: Swing Youth (mostly middle-class, Hamburg/Berlin, jazz from 1939); Edelweiss Pirates (working-class, Ruhr/Cologne, attacking HJ patrols, 12 hanged in Cologne 1944).
• Religious resistance: Niemoller imprisoned 1937–45; Bonhoeffer hanged at Flossenburg 9 April 1945; Galen's August 1941 sermon halting the official T4 programme; Catholic encyclical Mit brennender Sorge (1937).
• Student resistance: White Rose, Munich, 1942–43; six leaflets; Hans, Sophie Scholl and Probst executed by guillotine 22 February 1943; Huber and others followed.
• Conservative-military resistance: Beck, Goerdeler, Stauffenberg; Operation Valkyrie; bomb at Wolf's Lair 12:42pm on 20 July 1944; conspirators shot the same night; around 5,000 arrested.
• Limits and significance: no opposition removed Hitler; significance lies in preserving alternative Germany; Galen's sermon changed T4 policy; the Bendlerblock became post-war memorial; effectiveness vs significance is the key historiographical move.
• Conclusion: youth, religious, student and conservative resistance never combined into a single movement and never threatened the regime militarily. They were significant rather than effective — preserving moral and political alternatives that became foundational for the Federal Republic after 1945.
[Mastering (10-12): both bullets covered with developed examples and substantiated overall judgement. Secure (7-9): both covered with relevant detail. Developing (4-6): one bullet well or both superficially. Emerging (1-3): brief or generalised.]

practice_questions.text: Compare the views in Interpretation A (a 1990s historian arguing wartime opposition was driven mainly by revulsion at Nazi crimes against Jews and the disabled) and Interpretation B (a 2000s historian arguing wartime opposition was driven mainly by recognition that the war could not be won) on the motives of the July 1944 conspirators. What is the main difference between these views?
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Interpretation A frames the conspirators as morally driven — Holocaust knowledge, T4, Kristallnacht as the trigger.
• Interpretation B frames the conspirators as strategically driven — military defeat after Stalingrad, the bombing campaign, the prospect of Soviet occupation.
• Main difference: A sees moral revulsion as the engine; B sees calculation about war's outcome as the engine.
[Mastering (4): clear identification of the difference with specific support. Secure (3): identified with limited support. Developing (2): paraphrases each side. Emerging (1): summarises one only.]
